 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Surfers Scramble to California Hot Spot to Catch Building-Size Waves
 Amid back-to-back storms hitting the coast, surfers could get a rare opportunity to catch big waves.
 Listen · 4:25 min Share full article 
 Potential waves at Mavericks in Northern California are attracting hopeful surfers. Credit... Jenn Cain/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images By Amy Graff 
 Amy Graff is a reporter on The Times’s weather team. She is based in San Francisco.
 Nov. 13, 2026 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. Encuentra más de nuestra cobertura en los resultados de búsqueda. Add The New York Times as a preferred source on Google Agrega The New York Times como fuente preferida en Google › 
 Expert surfers around the world were busy rearranging their lives this week, hoping to get themselves to the Northern California coast by Saturday morning.
 Word had spread quickly among their close-knit surfing community that a swell in the Pacific was traveling thousands of miles across the ocean and was expected to bring mountains of water nearing 50 feet tall to Mavericks, a famed surf spot 20 miles south of San Francisco.
 If all goes well, the waves will arrive between two storms, offering surfers a small window of thrills, even as experts up and down the coast warned everyday people to stay away from beaches. Back-to-back storm systems are giving California its first widespread rain of the season , and widespread weather warnings for flooding and strong winds were in place. One storm was set to move on by Saturday morning, before another hits on Sunday.
 Big-wave riders scrambled to seize the moment, some with easier travel itineraries than others.
 On Thursday, Bianca Valenti, 41, was getting her gear ready at home in San Francisco and planned to drive to Mavericks on Saturday morning. Six thousand miles away, Clément Roseyro, 27, grabbed three surfboards and got on a plane early Friday morning in Biarritz in southern France.
 “It’s a big mission to get there on time with all the gear,” Mr. Roseyro said.
 Part of the gear prep was lining up a Jet Ski. The waves at Mavericks are so big that surfers are often thrown into them as they hold onto a rope attached to one of these 200-plus-horsepower machines driven by a surf partner.
 “Every serious big-wave surfer or big-wave filmer is trying to rent a Jet Ski right now and find a way to get out there,” Ms. Valenti said.
